screens.title: Displays: Character LCD and OLED
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we’ll make small displays work for real projects. You will learn how to wire and control a common 16x2 or 20x4 character LCD using the I2C interface, and how to use a monochrome SSD1306 OLED to draw text and simple shapes. We’ll cover the libraries you need, how to initialize a display, and practical tips for formatting sensor values so they stay readable. You’ll also see a short comparison between character LCDs and OLEDs so you know when to choose each type. A concrete use case is showing temperature and humidity from a DHT11 on a 16x2 display that updates every two seconds with labels and units. A common pitfall is updating too rapidly or forgetting to clear leftover characters; we’ll show how to avoid that. By the end you’ll understand wiring, the initialization pattern, how to control cursor position and text output, and how to present sensor data cleanly on a tiny screen. Think about where a small on-device display would save you time debugging without a laptop attached.

Displays: Character LCD and OLED

Wire via I2C, install the right library, and format sensor output so the screen stays clear and readable.

Text using character blocks. Common: 16x2, 20x4.

Quick Start Example
#include <LiquidCrystal_I2C.h>
LiquidCrystal_I2C lcd(0x27, 16, 2);

void setup() {

  lcd.backlight();
  lcd.setCursor(0, 0);

screens.title: Character LCDs: How they show text
screens.narratorSegment: A character LCD renders text by filling fixed character cells arranged in rows and columns. Typical modules are called 16 by 2 or 20 by 4, which means 16 columns and 2 rows, or 20 columns and 4 rows respectively. Each cell contains a predefined pixel pattern for letters, digits, and some symbols. Because characters are block-based, you cannot draw arbitrary shapes across the screen as you would on an OLED. A concrete example is printing the text "Temperature:" on a 16x2 module; you choose a column and row with a cursor function and then print the label and value. One common misconception is assuming the display automatically removes leftover characters when new text is shorter. In reality, if you overwrite a longer string with a shorter one, leftover characters remain unless you clear or overwrite them explicitly. That is why we use either a clear command or print spaces to erase old content. Practically, these displays are excellent for stable labels and numeric readouts, and they are easy to use in menus where text alignment matters. Think of character LCDs as tidy, limited canvases: predictable and very readable for short text, but not for graphics.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Character LCDs
Definition

How character LCDs render text

A character LCD maps characters to fixed cells. Each cell displays a glyph from the module's character set.

Key properties
  • Fixed grid: columns × rows (for example 16×2)
  • Predefined glyphs for letters/digits
  • Simple APIs: setCursor, print, clear
Common-mistake
Expecting automatic erasure when new text is shorter; remember to clear or overwrite.
Example
lcd.setCursor(0,0) // position
lcd.print("Temp:") // label
lcd.setCursor(0,1) // second row
lcd.print("23 C") // value
Takeaway
Use character LCDs for clear text readouts and labeled values.
Pro tip
When updating values, either clear line or print fixed-width fields to avoid leftovers.

screens.title: I2C wiring and why it helps
screens.narratorSegment: I2C simplifies connecting displays by using a shared two-wire data bus plus power. Instead of many parallel data pins, an I2C-equipped backpack exposes VCC, GND, SDA, and SCL. VCC and GND provide power. SDA is the serial data line and SCL is the clock line. A single I2C bus can support multiple devices as long as each has a unique address, commonly 0x27 or 0x3F for character LCD backpacks. The wiring process is straightforward: power the display, connect SDA to the board's SDA pin and SCL to SCL, then run an I2C scanner example to confirm the device address. The practical benefit is fewer GPIO pins used and simpler ribbon wiring for compact projects. A common misconception is that I2C automatically resolves address conflicts; you must ensure devices use different addresses or use an address multiplexer. For beginners, the verification step is to scan the bus, note the address, and use that address in your display library initialisation. After wiring, initialize the library and test a static message to confirm both power and communications are correct. I2C wiring and why it helps means i2c reduces many parallel pins to two shared lines, simplifying wiring and enabling multiple devices on the same bus.. In practical terms, use vcc, gnd, sda, and scl to reduce pins and tidy wiring. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › I2C Wiring
Process

Steps to wire and verify an I2C display

1
Attach power
Connect VCC to 5V (or 3.3V if appropriate) and GND to ground.
2
Connect data lines
Wire SDA to the board's SDA pin and SCL to SCL. Use pull-ups if your board lacks them.
3
Scan the bus
Run an I2C scanner sketch to find the device address, commonly 0x27 or 0x3F.
4
Initialize in code
Use the detected address when creating your display object so commands reach the device.
Why it matters

Fewer pins and simpler wiring make prototypes neater and free up microcontroller GPIO for sensors and controls. Multiple displays or sensors can share the same bus when addresses don't collide.

Common-mistake
Assuming address conflicts are resolved automatically; if two devices share an address you'll need an addressable module or multiplexer.
Check your understanding
After wiring, does the display power LED light and does an I2C scan return an address? If not, re-check SDA/SCL and power pins.

screens.title: Using LiquidCrystal_I2C
screens.narratorSegment: Using a character LCD over I2C follows a simple initialization pattern. After installing the LiquidCrystal_I2C library, you create a display object with the device address and the module dimensions. In setup you call initialization functions and enable the backlight if supported. The main loop then positions the cursor and uses the print function to send text. A practical example is printing elapsed seconds on the second row. Notice that printing numbers directly may leave leftover characters if digits shrink; to avoid this we either clear the line before printing or format the output to fixed width. For novices, an important contrast is that the LiquidCrystal_I2C library provides simple print and setCursor functions similar to the Serial print A P I, which makes it easy to transfer display output code from Serial to the screen. A concrete example walkthrough: create the object with 0x27 and 16,2; call init and backlight in setup; set cursor to column 0 row 0 to print a label; set cursor to row 1 for the numeric update. Finally, always test with an I2C scanner first to confirm the address before running display code.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › LiquidCrystal_I2C Walkthrough
Code Pattern
#include <LiquidCrystal_I2C.h>
LiquidCrystal_I2C lcd(0x27, 16, 2);

void setup() {
  lcd.init();
  lcd.backlight();
  lcd.setCursor(0,0);
  lcd.print("Temp:");
}

void loop() {
  lcd.setCursor(0,1);
  lcd.print(millis() / 1000);
  // clear or overwrite shorter text to avoid leftover chars
}
Explanation
  • lcd(0x27,16,2) — creates the object using the detected I2C address and dimensions.
  • lcd.init() — initializes the controller; required before commands.
  • lcd.backlight() — turns on backlight if supported by the backpack.
  • setCursor() — positions where subsequent prints will appear.
Example Scenario
Show elapsed seconds updating every two seconds with a fixed-width field to avoid residue.
Misconception
Assuming lcd.print replaces the entire line; shorter strings can leave old characters.

screens.title: Clearing and updating display text
screens.narratorSegment: Keeping a display readable requires thoughtful updates. When a new text string is shorter than the previous one, leftover characters remain unless you clear or overwrite them. There are three common approaches: clear the entire display before printing, overwrite with a fixed-width field or padded string, or explicitly write spaces over the remaining characters on the line. Clearing the entire display is simple but can cause visible flicker if done too often. Overwriting with fixed-width fields avoids flicker and keeps alignment; for numeric values, format them to a fixed precision or pad with spaces. Another concern is refresh rate: updating many times per second can create visible flicker and stress the bus. A practical rule is to refresh only when values change significantly or at a moderate interval, like once per second or every two seconds for slowly changing sensors. A concrete example: showing temperature with one decimal place and updating only when the value changes by at least 0.1 degrees reduces unnecessary refreshes. Remember that clearing and reprinting should be balanced with the human perception of updates. Clearing and updating display text means either clear carefully, overwrite with fixed widths, or limit refresh frequency to keep the display clean and steady.. In practical terms, avoid leftover characters and flicker when updating values. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Clearing & Updating
Approaches
Clear display
Call clear before printing. Simple but can flicker if used frequently.
Overwrite with fixed width
Format values to fixed length or pad with spaces to fully overwrite previous text.
Conditional refresh
Only update when the value changes beyond a threshold or at a controlled interval to reduce flicker.
Concrete Example
Show temperature to one decimal place and update only when it changes by 0.1 degrees. If new text shorter than previous, write trailing spaces to erase remnants.
Check your understanding
If the previous value was "100.00" and the new value is "99.9", what will you see unless you clear or pad? There will be leftover characters like a hanging "0" at the end.

screens.title: OLED (SSD1306) vs Character LCD
screens.narratorSegment: OLED displays with the SSD1306 driver are pixel-addressable, which means you can draw shapes, small icons, and text at arbitrary positions. This flexibility contrasts with character LCDs, which confine you to predefined glyphs in a grid. In practical terms, an OLED is great for simple graphics like a battery icon, progress bar, or compact status line; a character LCD is a straightforward choice for labeled numerical readouts and menus. OLEDs typically have better contrast and no backlight, so they remain readable at many angles. A concrete example: a 0.96-inch SSD1306 can draw a small rectangle as a graph and print a number inside it, while a 16x2 LCD cannot place that number inside a drawn box without creative character patterns. One misconception is that OLEDs always require more wiring or complexity; they also use I2C and are nearly identical in wiring. Choose OLED when you need pixel-level control or compact graphics; choose character LCD when you prefer simpler text-only output and lower code complexity. Consider power use as a practical factor for battery projects. In practical terms, when to pick pixels over character blocks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Pixel-addressable, supports text and shapes, high contrast, draws graphics such as icons and small plots.

Status bar with icons and a tiny graph next to a numeric readout.

screens.title: SSD1306 OLED basics with Adafruit library
screens.narratorSegment: Working with an SSD1306 OLED uses a buffer-based approach: you draw pixels, shapes, or text to an internal buffer and then call a display function to push the buffer to the screen. After installing the Adafruit SSD1306 and GFX libraries, you create the display object with the correct I2C address and dimensions, call begin in setup, and then use drawing helpers to compose the frame. For example, draw a rectangle to represent a status box, set a text cursor and print a value, then call the display update function to render everything at once. This reduces flicker compared to clearing and drawing separate elements. A practical example: draw a small rectangle and then print a numeric sensor value inside it. A frequent misconception is trying to directly manipulate pixels without updating the buffer; remember to call the method that sends the buffer to the physical screen. Another tip is to limit the size and frequency of buffer updates for power efficiency. Overall, the OLED gives more control and expressive possibilities than a character LCD while keeping I2C wiring simple.   • Buffered updates — draw everything to memory and call display once per frame.
  • Drawing helpers — use drawPixel, drawLine, drawRect, and setTextSize for layout.
  • No backlight — OLEDs are emissive; contrast is typically high without a backlight.
Example Scenario
Draw a progress bar by filling a rectangle proportionally, then print a number above it. Update the buffer less frequently to save power.

screens.title: Formatting sensor output cleanly
screens.narratorSegment: Formatting sensor output is crucial for readability. Floating-point numbers can print with many decimal places by default, which makes small screens noisy. Use formatting functions to control how many digits appear. Two common approaches on Arduino are converting values into formatted strings with a function that controls precision, or using a helper like dtostrf to create a fixed-width text buffer. For simple integer displays, cast or round values before printing. Another technique is to build a label string and reserve a fixed width for the numeric field so updates overwrite previous digits cleanly. For example, when showing humidity at one decimal place, format the value to one decimal and ensure the printed field is padded to a fixed length. A common misconception is that adding format control will slow down the loop significantly; in most beginner projects it's negligible compared to sensor read time. Also, avoid updating the display on every loop iteration; update when the value changes beyond a threshold or on a timed interval, such as every two seconds for a DHT11. This reduces flicker and prevents overwhelming the I2C bus.

keyIdea.title: Readable numbers
keyIdea.text: Format numbers to a sensible precision and reserve fixed-width fields so successive prints overwrite previous text cleanly.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Formatting Output
Why formatting matters

Small screens must be concise. Limiting decimal places and reserving space for numbers keeps readouts tidy and predictable.

Use fixed precision for floats so "23.123456" becomes "23.1" or "23.12" depending on readability needs.
Build strings with padding or use dtostrf to ensure fixed-width number fields.
Refresh only on meaningful change or at a moderate interval to avoid flicker and bus congestion.
Concrete Example
If a humidity sensor returns 46.789, format to one decimal as "46.8%" and update only if value changed by 0.1 or after two seconds. Pad to three characters for alignment: " 6.8" vs "46.8".
Gotcha
Printing floats without formatting often leads to long, unreadable numbers and display clutter.

screens.title: Hands-on: DHT11 → 16x2 I2C LCD activity
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on flow shows how to wire a DHT11 sensor and display temperature and humidity on a 16x2 I2C LCD. First, wire power and ground for both the sensor and display. Connect SDA and SCL from the display to the board's bus; the DHT11 uses a single data pin to a digital input on the microcontroller. Second, run an I2C scanner to find the display address and use that address in the LiquidCrystal_I2C constructor. Third, in setup initialize the display and the DHT library. In the loop, read the sensor, format temperature and humidity values to a sensible precision, and compare current readings to the previous ones. Only update the display when values change or on a two-second timer to reduce flicker. Make sure to clear or overwrite shorter strings, and add labels like "T:" and "H:" so values are self-explanatory. A common beginner mistake is updating too fast or forgetting units; test the flow and ask: does the display show stable labels and readable numbers every two seconds? If yes, the activity is complete and the device can run standalone for local monitoring.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › DHT11 to LCD Activity
Wiring & Setup
  1. Power: connect VCC and GND for both display and DHT11.
  2. I2C: wire SDA and SCL from the display to the SDA/SCL pins of the board.
  3. Sensor: connect the DHT11 data pin to a digital input and a pull-up if needed.
  4. Code: run I2C scanner, then use the found address in your LiquidCrystal_I2C constructor.
Example Labels
Row 0: "T: 23.4 C" Row 1: "H: 46.8 %" — include units for clarity.
Loop Strategy
Read sensor every two seconds. Format values, compare with previous readings, and update the display only when changed or on the timer to avoid flicker and bus congestion.
Assessment Idea
Ask: Why is I2C preferred over parallel wiring for LCDs? Expected answer: It uses fewer pins and simplifies wiring while supporting multiple devices on the same bus.

Second, I2C simplifies wiring to four wires — VCC, GND, SDA, and SCL — and enables multiple devices on one bus, but watch for address collisions. Third, SSD1306 OLEDs are pixel-addressable and let you draw shapes and small graphics; use the Adafruit libraries to draw to a buffer and push the frame. Each concept maps to practical steps: scan the bus to find an address, initialize the library, format numbers for readability, and choose an update cadence that avoids flicker. As you practice, use the display not only to show readings but also to debug when a computer is not connected. Which display will you choose for your next project, and why?

screens.title: Essentials & Quick Checks
screens.narratorSegment: Keep these quick checks in mind as you work. First, always run an I2C scanner before relying on an address in code; it saves time and confusion. Second, format numeric output to a sensible precision and reserve fixed-width fields to avoid trailing characters. Third, use buffered updates for OLEDs so you compose frames in memory and call a single display update. Each check maps to a small action: scan, format, and buffer. These actions prevent common errors like address mismatches, unreadable numbers, and flicker. Try asking yourself after each change: can I reproduce this on the screen, and does it remain readable after several updates? That habit will help you build reliable, user-friendly projects with tiny displays. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we’ll make small displays work for real projects. You will learn how to wire and control a common 16x2 or 20x4 character LCD using the I2C interface, and how to use a monochrome SSD1306 OLED to draw text and simple shapes. We’ll cover the libraries you need, how to initialize a display, and practical tips for formatting sensor values so they stay readable. You’ll also see a short comparison between character LCDs and OLEDs so you know when to choose each type. A concrete use case is showing temperature and humidity from a DHT11 on a 16x2 display that updates every two seconds with labels and units. A common pitfall is updating too rapidly or forgetting to clear leftover characters; we’ll show how to avoid that. By the end you’ll understand wiring, the initialization pattern, how to control cursor position and text output, and how to present sensor data cleanly on a tiny screen. Think about where a small on-device display would save you time debugging without a laptop attached.

These objectives give you hands-on, practical skills you can use immediately. First, you will learn how to connect and control a 16x2 or 20x4 character LCD using an I2C backpack. That means understanding the four-wire connection and why addresses like 0x27 or 0x3F matter. Second, you will learn to display sensor data and messages: position the cursor, print text, and update values without leaving artifacts on the screen. Third, you will use a monochrome OLED with the SSD1306 driver to draw text and simple shapes, which expands possibilities beyond fixed character blocks. Fourth, you'll practice formatting output so numbers are easy to read, controlling decimal places and refresh rate to prevent flicker. Each objective includes a small mnemonic and a verified competency milestone so you can check off the skill. These outcomes are useful for debugging, creating simple user interfaces, and building standalone sensor displays for projects that do not run attached to a computer.

This page breaks each objective into practical verification steps. For wiring, you will measure that the display powers on and responds to a scan with a known I2C address. For display output, you will position labels and values so they remain stable when updated. For the OLED, you will draw a short status bar and a numeric value to see pixel-level control. For formatting, you will choose how many decimal places to show and implement a strategy to clear or overwrite old text so characters don't remain when new values are shorter. Each objective ties to a small exercise: connect a display, print two labeled values, show a simple OLED graphic, and format values to two decimal places or to an integer when appropriate. A common misconception is that displays automatically erase characters; in many cases you must explicitly clear or overwrite. These verification steps help you prove competence and avoid that trap.

A character LCD renders text by filling fixed character cells arranged in rows and columns. Typical modules are called 16 by 2 or 20 by 4, which means 16 columns and 2 rows, or 20 columns and 4 rows respectively. Each cell contains a predefined pixel pattern for letters, digits, and some symbols. Because characters are block-based, you cannot draw arbitrary shapes across the screen as you would on an OLED. A concrete example is printing the text "Temperature:" on a 16x2 module; you choose a column and row with a cursor function and then print the label and value. One common misconception is assuming the display automatically removes leftover characters when new text is shorter. In reality, if you overwrite a longer string with a shorter one, leftover characters remain unless you clear or overwrite them explicitly. That is why we use either a clear command or print spaces to erase old content. Practically, these displays are excellent for stable labels and numeric readouts, and they are easy to use in menus where text alignment matters. Think of character LCDs as tidy, limited canvases: predictable and very readable for short text, but not for graphics.

I2C simplifies connecting displays by using a shared two-wire data bus plus power. Instead of many parallel data pins, an I2C-equipped backpack exposes VCC, GND, SDA, and SCL. VCC and GND provide power. SDA is the serial data line and SCL is the clock line. A single I2C bus can support multiple devices as long as each has a unique address, commonly 0x27 or 0x3F for character LCD backpacks. The wiring process is straightforward: power the display, connect SDA to the board's SDA pin and SCL to SCL, then run an I2C scanner example to confirm the device address. The practical benefit is fewer GPIO pins used and simpler ribbon wiring for compact projects. A common misconception is that I2C automatically resolves address conflicts; you must ensure devices use different addresses or use an address multiplexer. For beginners, the verification step is to scan the bus, note the address, and use that address in your display library initialisation. After wiring, initialize the library and test a static message to confirm both power and communications are correct. I2C wiring and why it helps means i2c reduces many parallel pins to two shared lines, simplifying wiring and enabling multiple devices on the same bus.. In practical terms, use vcc, gnd, sda, and scl to reduce pins and tidy wiring. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Using a character LCD over I2C follows a simple initialization pattern. After installing the LiquidCrystal_I2C library, you create a display object with the device address and the module dimensions. In setup you call initialization functions and enable the backlight if supported. The main loop then positions the cursor and uses the print function to send text. A practical example is printing elapsed seconds on the second row. Notice that printing numbers directly may leave leftover characters if digits shrink; to avoid this we either clear the line before printing or format the output to fixed width. For novices, an important contrast is that the LiquidCrystal_I2C library provides simple print and setCursor functions similar to the Serial print A P I, which makes it easy to transfer display output code from Serial to the screen. A concrete example walkthrough: create the object with 0x27 and 16,2; call init and backlight in setup; set cursor to column 0 row 0 to print a label; set cursor to row 1 for the numeric update. Finally, always test with an I2C scanner first to confirm the address before running display code.

Keeping a display readable requires thoughtful updates. When a new text string is shorter than the previous one, leftover characters remain unless you clear or overwrite them. There are three common approaches: clear the entire display before printing, overwrite with a fixed-width field or padded string, or explicitly write spaces over the remaining characters on the line. Clearing the entire display is simple but can cause visible flicker if done too often. Overwriting with fixed-width fields avoids flicker and keeps alignment; for numeric values, format them to a fixed precision or pad with spaces. Another concern is refresh rate: updating many times per second can create visible flicker and stress the bus. A practical rule is to refresh only when values change significantly or at a moderate interval, like once per second or every two seconds for slowly changing sensors. A concrete example: showing temperature with one decimal place and updating only when the value changes by at least 0.1 degrees reduces unnecessary refreshes. Remember that clearing and reprinting should be balanced with the human perception of updates. In practical terms, avoid leftover characters and flicker when updating values. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

OLED displays with the SSD1306 driver are pixel-addressable, which means you can draw shapes, small icons, and text at arbitrary positions. This flexibility contrasts with character LCDs, which confine you to predefined glyphs in a grid. In practical terms, an OLED is great for simple graphics like a battery icon, progress bar, or compact status line; a character LCD is a straightforward choice for labeled numerical readouts and menus. OLEDs typically have better contrast and no backlight, so they remain readable at many angles. A concrete example: a 0.96-inch SSD1306 can draw a small rectangle as a graph and print a number inside it, while a 16x2 LCD cannot place that number inside a drawn box without creative character patterns. Choose OLED when you need pixel-level control or compact graphics; choose character LCD when you prefer simpler text-only output and lower code complexity. Consider power use as a practical factor for battery projects. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Working with an SSD1306 OLED uses a buffer-based approach: you draw pixels, shapes, or text to an internal buffer and then call a display function to push the buffer to the screen. After installing the Adafruit SSD1306 and GFX libraries, you create the display object with the correct I2C address and dimensions, call begin in setup, and then use drawing helpers to compose the frame. Another tip is to limit the size and frequency of buffer updates for power efficiency. Overall, the OLED gives more control and expressive possibilities than a character LCD while keeping I2C wiring simple.
